e2e.output:
I can’t honestly give you a “good borscht recipe with **exact proportions**” from the material I was able to retrieve, because the accessible recipes I found (Alyona’s Cooking, Once Upon a Chef, NYT Cooking) all rely partly on **non-exact measures** like “1 medium onion / 2 medium carrots,” and I was **not able to retrieve** an authoritative source (e.g., USDA FoodData Central portion weights) to convert those into exact grams in a properly cited way. Also, the tool output I could access did **not include yield/servings** for those recipes.

Rather than invent gram weights (which would defeat “exact proportions”), here is the best I can do **strictly from sourced amounts**: a well-regarded Ukrainian-style borscht recipe with exact *as-published* proportions, plus the method.

---

## Ukrainian-style borscht (sourced proportions; US measures)

### Ingredients (exactly as published)
From Once Upon a Chef “Borscht”:

- Olive oil: **1 Tbsp**  
- Onion: **1 medium**, chopped  
- Celery: **1 rib**, finely chopped  
- Beef broth: **6 cups**  
- Green cabbage: **4 cups (10 oz) lightly packed**, thinly sliced  
- Beets: **1 lb**, peeled and diced (¾-inch / 2-cm pieces)  
- Tomato paste: **1/4 cup**  
- Bay leaf: **1**  
- Salt: **1 1/4 tsp**  
- Black pepper: **1/4 tsp**  
- Potatoes: **2 large Yukon gold (about 1 lb / 454 g)**, cubed (½-inch)  
- Carrots: **2 medium**, diced (½-inch)  
- Distilled white vinegar: **1 Tbsp**  
- To serve: **2 Tbsp chopped dill**, sour cream

### Method (exactly as published, condensed)
1. Sauté onion + celery in oil **5–7 min**.  
2. Add broth, cabbage, beets, tomato paste, bay leaf, salt, pepper; bring to a boil. Cover and **simmer 10 min**.  
3. Add potatoes + carrots; return to a boil. Cover and cook **~20 min** until tender.  
4. Discard bay leaf; **stir in vinegar at the end**. Serve with dill + sour cream.

**Source:** https://www.onceuponachef.com/recipes/borscht.html (also accessible via `#print-recipe`)

---

## Conclusions
- I can provide a “good borscht” recipe with **precise as-published measures**, but I **cannot** provide a fully metric (grams/ml) recipe with truly exact produce weights from the sources I could access, because:
  - the recipes use “medium” produce without gram equivalents, and  
  - authoritative conversion pages (USDA/FDC portion weights) were not extractable with the available tooling in this run.
- If you tell me whether you want **(A)** beef borscht or **(B)** vegetarian borscht, and your **target yield** (e.g., “exactly 3.0 L”), I can either:
  1) produce an “exact grams/ml” recipe **using your own weighed produce** (you weigh your onion/carrot/etc. and I’ll give exact ratios for the rest), or  
  2) try again to locate a **metric-native recipe source** (UK/EU) that publishes grams/ml + servings in accessible text.

## Sources
- Once Upon a Chef — “Borscht”: https://www.onceuponachef.com/recipes/borscht.html

## What I did (research actions)
- Ran multiple **web_search** queries for “Ukrainian borscht recipe” focusing on **exact quantities** (grams/ml), yield, and critical technique (beet treatment, vinegar/acid, simmer times). Some searches failed due to connection/timeouts (documented below).
- Opened and extracted full text from 3 accessible, reputable recipe pages using **read_url**:
  1) **Alyona’s Cooking** (explicit “Authentic Ukrainian Borscht Recipe” with quarts/cups/lbs and step times)  
  2) **Once Upon a Chef** (Ukrainian-style, with weights for key items and clear method)  
  3) **NYT Cooking** “Winter Borscht” (classic beef borscht; ingredient quantities + detailed multi-stage simmering)

## Key findings (recipes with sourced quantities, yield notes, and critical techniques)

### Source 1 — Alyona’s Cooking: “Authentic Ukrainian Borscht Recipe”
**Ingredient quantities (as published)**
- Beef chuck roast: **1 1/2 lb** (boneless), cut into 1-inch pieces  
- Water: **3 1/2 quarts (14 cups)**  
- Potatoes: **6 medium golden potatoes = 2 1/2 lb**, peeled/cubed  
- Salt: **1 Tbsp**  
- Sauerkraut: **1 cup** *(or “2 cups fresh shredded cabbage + 1 Tbsp white distilled vinegar”)*  
- Mirepoix/zazharka: **2 medium carrots**, **1 large onion**, **2 large beets**, **8 oz tomato sauce**, **2 Tbsp olive oil**  
- Seasonings: **1 Tbsp Vegeta**, **1/2 tsp black pepper**, **1 Tbsp garlic salt**, **3 bay leaves**  
- Garnish: sour cream + dill (amounts “as desired”)  
**Source:** https://www.alyonascooking.com/easy-borscht-recipe-beet-soup/

**Method + critical technique (as published)**
- Boil beef in water, skim foam, **simmer 30 min**.  
- Add potatoes + salt; **simmer 25 min** (less if smaller dice).  
- Make **zazharka**: sauté onion + grated beets + carrots in oil **~10 min**, add tomato sauce, then add to soup.  
- After potatoes: add seasonings + bay + sauerkraut; **simmer 7 min**.  
- Technique note: **“Pickled or roasted beets get added at the end… to keep their red color.”** (they also describe how raw beets are handled differently).  
**Source:** https://www.alyonascooking.com/easy-borscht-recipe-beet-soup/

**Yield**
- Not explicitly stated as servings/liters on the captured page text; however the recipe uses **3.5 quarts / 14 cups water** as the base liquid, implying a large pot.  
**Source for the measurable base volume:** https://www.alyonascooking.com/easy-borscht-recipe-beet-soup/  
**What I did NOT find:** an explicit “serves X” or “makes Y quarts” statement in the extracted text.

---

### Source 2 — Once Upon a Chef: “Borscht” (Ukrainian-style)
**Ingredient quantities (as published; includes weights for several items)**
- Olive oil: **1 Tbsp**  
- Onion: **1 medium**, chopped  
- Celery: **1 rib**, finely chopped  
- Beef broth: **6 cups**  
- Green cabbage: **4 cups (10 oz) lightly packed**, thinly sliced  
- Beets: **1 lb**, peeled and diced (¾-inch / 2-cm pieces)  
- Tomato paste: **1/4 cup**  
- Bay leaf: **1**  
- Salt: **1 1/4 tsp**  
- Black pepper: **1/4 tsp**  
- Potatoes: **2 large Yukon gold (~1 lb / 454 g)**, cubed (½-inch)  
- Carrots: **2 medium**, diced (½-inch)  
- Distilled white vinegar: **1 Tbsp**  
- Dill for serving: **2 Tbsp chopped**; sour cream for serving  
**Source:** https://www.onceuponachef.com/recipes/borscht.html

**Method + critical technique (as published)**
- Sauté onion + celery in oil **5–7 min**.  
- Add broth + cabbage + beets + tomato paste + bay + salt/pepper; bring to boil, then **cover & simmer 10 min**.  
- Add potatoes + carrots; return to boil then **cover & cook ~20 min** until tender.  
- Discard bay leaf; **stir in vinegar at the end**.  
- Technique notes include: staggered veg cooking to avoid mush; vinegar to “brighten” and adjust if flat.  
**Source:** https://www.onceuponachef.com/recipes/borscht.html

**Yield**
- Not captured in the extracted text (likely present in the printable recipe card, but not explicitly shown in the tool output).  
**What I did NOT find:** explicit servings or final volume in the extracted content.

---

### Source 3 — NYT Cooking: “Winter Borscht”
**Ingredient quantities (as published)**
- Beef shin with bone: **2 lb** (2-inch pieces)  
- Water for initial stock: **6 cups**  
- Onion: **1 small**, halved  
- Carrots: **2 medium** (1 quartered, 1 grated)  
- Red beets: **3 medium**  
- Tomato paste: **6 Tbsp**  
- Garlic: **4 medium cloves**  
- Red cabbage: **1/2 lb**, shredded  
- Tomatoes: **2 medium**  
- Bay leaf: **1**  
- Red-wine vinegar: **2 Tbsp**  
- Sugar: **2 Tbsp + 2 tsp**  
- Potatoes: **1 lb**, peeled, cubed; cooked separately in salted water until tender  
- Kosher salt: **2 tsp**; pepper to taste  
- Dill: **1/3 cup chopped** (+ more for garnish)  
- Garnish: sour cream; optional **1/2 boiled firm potato per person**  
**Source:** https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/6910-winter-borscht

**Method + critical technique (as published)**
- Simmer beef with onion + quartered carrot in **6 cups water**; **1 hr 30 min**, then strain; target **~4 1/2 cups** liquid.  
- Cook whole beets in broth **~20 min**, cool/peel/grate, return grated beets to soup.  
- Dissolve tomato paste in **1/2 cup soup**, add back; add garlic, grated carrot, cabbage, tomatoes, bay, vinegar, sugar; **simmer 1 hr 30 min**.  
- Debone/slice meat; add meat + cooked potatoes + salt/pepper + dill; boil **2 min**.  
**Source:** https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/6910-winter-borscht

**Yield**
- Not shown in the extracted text (NYT often displays yield separately; not present in tool output).  
**What I did NOT find:** explicit yield/servings in the extracted content.

---

## Gaps / what I did not find (actionable)
- **Metric-precise Ukrainian borscht recipes (grams/ml throughout)** from mainstream sites: the three sources above mix US volume/imperial with a few weights (not full grams/ml across all ingredients). (Evidence: ingredient lists as captured from each URL above.)
- **Servings/yield** values were **not captured** in the extracted text for Alyona’s Cooking, Once Upon a Chef, or NYT Cooking (even though they may exist on-page in sections not returned by the tool output).  
  - NYT Cooking is also sometimes paywalled/structured; I could access ingredient/method text but not yield in the returned content. Source: https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/6910-winter-borscht
- Attempted to retrieve a second mainstream borscht page (**Simply Recipes**) but it was **blocked/unavailable** via the tool.  
  - **Not found due to access failure:** Simply Recipes borscht full text. Tool result: “page … unavailable (timeout, 403/404, or blocked).” Source attempt: https://www.simplyrecipes.com/recipes/borscht/
- Several **web_search** queries failed due to DNS/timeouts, limiting discovery of cookbook-based metric recipes. Tool errors recorded:
  - DNS/connect error on a Ukrainian borscht grams/ml query (web_search failure).
  - Timeouts on queries targeting Olga’s Flavor Factory / Natasha’s Kitchen specifically.

These findings should be sufficient to draft a reliable “exact proportions” recipe by converting the published weights/volumes into grams/ml, but **a fully metric-native source** (all ingredients in grams/ml + explicit yield) was **not located** with the current tool access and the failed searches.

---

## 2) Authoritative references for typical weights of “medium onion”, “medium carrot”, “celery rib”, and tomato paste tbsp→grams (USDA FoodData Central or similar)

### USDA FoodData Central (FDC) accessibility status
- I was able to access the **FDC homepage** and its citation/licensing text.  
  **Source:** https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/
- However, attempts to use FDC’s **food-search pages** (onion/carrot/celery queries) returned only a short “Foundation Foods” landing snippet in the extracted text, **without any portion weights (e.g., ‘1 medium onion = X g’)**.  
  **Sources (all short/insufficient in tool output):**
  - https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-search/?query=onion  
  - https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-search/?query=carrot  
  - https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-search/?query=celery  

**Finding:** With the current tool extraction, I **cannot obtain** the needed per-unit gram weights directly from USDA FDC pages.

### Non-USDA sources surfaced by search (but not verified as authoritative)
Search did return some third-party “guides” claiming USDA-derived values (e.g., “medium onion ~130 g”), but these are not USDA primary sources. I have **not** opened and verified their internal citations in this run, and they are not “authoritative” per your request.
- Example search results pointing to third-party pages (not USDA): “Onion Weight Guide…” etc.  
  **Source (search results list):** web_search output for “USDA FoodData Central medium onion weight grams 1 medium” (no single authoritative USDA page extracted)

### Tomato paste tablespoon → grams
- Attempts to web_search specifically for “tomato paste tablespoon grams USDA” **timed out** in this run, so I did not retrieve a usable conversion reference page.  
  **Evidence:** tool error on that query (timeout) from the parallel run that also fetched FDC pages.

**What I did NOT find (explicitly):**
- A primary-source USDA/FDC page extractable by the tools that states:
  - “1 medium onion = ___ g”
  - “1 medium carrot = ___ g”
  - “1 celery rib/stalk = ___ g”
  - “1 tablespoon tomato paste = ___ g”

---

## 3) If no fully-metric recipe is accessible: can we still express Once Upon a Chef fully in grams/ml and estimate yield?

### What I can and cannot do with sources available
- I **can** cite Once Upon a Chef’s ingredient list, which already includes some weights:
  - cabbage: “4 cups (10 oz)”
  - beets: “1 lb”
  - potatoes: “about 1 lb/454 g”
  **Source:** https://www.onceuponachef.com/recipes/borscht.html#print-recipe
- But I **cannot** complete “fully in grams/ml” with authoritative conversions because:
  1) Once Upon a Chef does **not** give weights for “1 medium onion,” “1 rib celery,” “2 medium carrots,” etc. (in the extracted content).  
     **Source:** https://www.onceuponachef.com/recipes/borscht.html#print-recipe
  2) I do **not** have accessible authoritative conversion references (USDA FDC per-unit weights) from tool-extractable pages in this run (see Section 2).
  3) Estimating yield from “6 cups broth + veg volume” would require density/volume assumptions for chopped vegetables and/or finished-soup yield norms; I did **not** retrieve any authoritative references for those assumptions in this run due to search timeouts.

### NYT yield check (related)
- NYT Cooking “Winter Borscht” remains accessible for ingredients/steps but **yield/servings is not present** in the extracted text, so I cannot use it as a yield reference either.  
  **Source:** https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/6910-winter-borscht?smid=ck-recipe-iOS-share

---

## Bottom line (actionable gaps)
1) **Metric borscht recipe with explicit yield**: not found due to repeated web_search DNS/timeouts for UK/EU queries.
2) **Authoritative unit weights (USDA/FDC)**: FDC is accessible at the homepage level, but the tool extraction of search results does not expose the portion-weight data needed; therefore, those conversions remain un-sourced.
3) Without (1) or (2), I cannot responsibly produce a fully grams/ml version of Once Upon a Chef with proper citations, nor a sourced yield estimate.

If you want me to continue, the most direct next steps would be:
- Target a small set of specific UK/EU recipe sites known to publish metric cards (and try direct URL reads rather than searching), and/or
- Use an alternate authoritative database that presents portion weights in static HTML (more extractable than FDC’s interactive UI), **if you have preferred candidates**.
